title: Tips for Starting Pop-Up Debates Well
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a YouTube comment from a colleague named Connie Fletcher, Stuart uses her description of introducing Pop-Up Debates to seventh graders as a model for how to launch the strategy well. Fletcher's plan starts by calling the activity simply a "pop-up" rather than a "pop-up debate," beginning with low-stakes personal trivia before moving students from short phrases to full sentences via a sentence stem. Stuart praises this approach not because it matches his own progression exactly, but because it directly addresses the real first hurdle -- students' anxiety about public speaking -- through a low floor for participation and a clear sense of where the routine is headed. He explicitly says he likes her version more than his own precisely because it's hers: thoughtful, smart, and something she's genuinely excited about. In a postscript, he models how he honors a student's speaking accommodation during Pop-Up Debates, inviting rather than requiring participation.
points: Fletcher's technique for lowering the public-speaking barrier is to strip the word "debate" from the activity's name at first, softening it to a game-like "pop-up" before students ever have to argue a real position.
Her participation bar starts as low as standing and saying a single word or phrase, only later progressing to full sentences built from a sentence stem -- a deliberate low-to-high scaffold.

Stuart's larger point is that a teacher who adapts a strategy thoughtfully and makes it genuinely their own will out-perform someone who copies his exact version, because ownership and excitement carry through into execution.

His postscript on accommodations shows the practice in action: inviting rather than requiring a student with a speaking accommodation to participate, while working toward an eventual moment of participation on the student's own terms.
quotes: One of my classes is seventh grade social studies, and this will be my first year to try pop-up debates. I'm going to start by just calling it a pop-up the first few times, kind of like a game.
Once I get them used to popping up with super short phrases, I'll move on to full sentences from a sentence stem. I'm really excited to use this in my classroom!
She's aware of the initial hurdle: kids' anxiety about public speaking. To help her students overcome this hurdle, she's doing a few smart things.
While Connie's approach to helping kids over that public speaking anxiety hurdle is different from mine, I gotta tell ya, colleague: I like hers more.
Why? Because it's hers. Because it's smart. Because she's excited about it. And because it's going to work.

I pulled this student aside, explained Pop-Up Debates, and told the student they are invited to participate but not required to do so. I'm hoping that, before the semester is through, this student will experience the success of standing up during a PUD.
